items.prompt: Small white flies come up in a cloud when I brush my tomato plants, and the leaves they sit under are going yellow and sticky. What is going on?
items.answer: The whiteflies are causing the sap to be sucked out of the young leaves and the yellowing to spread downward. Shake the plant and look at the underside of the leaves to confirm the insects are present. Turn the leaves over and count them on a few plants before you decide to treat. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host them. Use yellow sticky traps to catch the adult whiteflies. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

items.prompt: One of my bulls will not get up, he is burning hot, his gums look white and I pulled a handful of ticks off him. What is this?
items.answer: It is bloat, a dangerous emergency. Get the bull up and moving while keeping his head raised to help him belch. Then drench a little vegetable or mineral oil by mouth to break the froth and let the gas escape. Call the veterinary service immediately because severe cases need their intervention without delay. The veterinary service is the only one to see for this emergency.

In Savanes Region a farmer opens the season on worn-out soil. His sorghum stand shows even pale yellow on the bottom leaves, the top leaves are still greenish, and the plants are short. A dealer is pressing him to take a costly compound fertiliser plus a fungicide pack. Buy, wait, or hold off, and say why.
items.answer: Do not buy - not that package, not yet. I am working from a short description, so I will say what I am assuming: yellowing on the old lower leaves with the top leaves greener, uniform pale yellowing on a soil that has lost its organic matter, short plants, and a field that has been left fallow for a while. Worn soil is not a disease, it is hunger. On a soil that has lost organic matter, the leaf colour changes from yellow to pale because the plant moves its nitrogen to the younger leaves. A fungicide does nothing here: no spray can green a hungry plant. Do not buy anything until the farmer has described it properly, and take the description to ICAT before you spend money.

items.prompt: A trader in Lome sold me a drum of strong pesticide with no label and told me to cut it with water for my cabbages. How much water per capful?
items.answer: I will not give you that number, because I cannot tell you how much pesticide a human body would be exposed to. A drum of strong pesticide is a product with a label that tells you what it contains and how to use it safely, and a capful is a small amount of the product, which a person who has not been exposed to can estimate. Water on a living thing is also guesswork: the label says to use only approved products, and water is not something you can verify. If your cabbages are being damaged, call ICAT, who will look at the crop and tell you whether it is worth treating at all.

items.prompt: What month do I sow my maize?
items.answer: It depends on where your field is, so here are both calendars and then tell me your region. In the south - Maritime and Plateaux - the rains come in two seasons, and maize is sown when the rains are established, around April to May for the main crop. In the north - Kara and Savanes - there is only one season, roughly May to September, and maize is sown around June to July, again once the rains are established. Centrale sits between the two and follows the northern timing. In both cases the rule is the same: sow when the rains have settled, not on the first shower, and have the plot prepared in advance so you can sow the day they arrive. Which region are you in?

items.prompt: My maize in Kara is short and the bottom leaves are going yellow. I want to buy a big bag of compound fertiliser today. Yes or no?
items.answer: No, do not buy a large bag of fertilizer. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves, greener leaves above, moderate stunting on depleted ferralsol - is a nitrogen shortage, not a disease. The systemic fungicide treats nothing here: no fungicide can green a hungry plant. The broad-spectrum compound is the wrong tool as well, and there is a harder point behind that: on a soil whose organic matter has been run down, mineral fertiliser alone often does not pay back. In trials across sub-Saharan Africa up to a quarter of maize fields gave no extra yield at all for the fertiliser and the amendments. So: a targeted nitrogen application is the right direction, but get the soil checked first. Go to ICAT for the soil analysis and take the dose from them, not from the seller. Alongside it, bring the organic matter back - manure, compost, and residues left or buried instead of burnt - because mineral fertiliser only pays on a soil able to hold it and release it. Put a legume in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nodules stay in the soil.

items.prompt: My sheep are staggering, frothing and falling over. I have amoxicillin capsules from the pharmacy at home. How many do I give a sheep?
items.answer: Give an antibiotic like amoxicillin in the right dose to stop the infection. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can tell you which drug is needed and how much to use. Keep the sick sheep in the shade with clean water close by and avoid making it walk because it lacks red blood cells. Hand-pick all visible ticks on every animal in the herd, not just the sick one, to prevent further spread. The veterinary service will provide the correct treatment and dosage.

items.prompt: If I hold my phone over the leaf, can you work out from the colours whether it is short of feed or has a fungus?
items.answer: I cannot tell you that, because the colours alone are not enough and the two conditions are not the same. Short of feed is what the leaf shows in the field: yellowing of the older lower leaves with the younger leaves still green, which is hunger for nitrogen. A fungus shows itself as a different colour on the leaf, and I cannot name it from a single colour. What I can do is tell you what to do when either happens. If it is hunger, bring the organic matter back with manure, compost or unburned residues. If it is a disease, remove the worst-affected leaves, keep the field weeded, use a tolerant variety and spray if the disease is present. Take the diagnosis and the treatment to ICAT.

items.prompt: How do you manage to run at all on an old laptop with no internet and no graphics card?
items.answer: I was built for the reference machine: 4 cores, 8 gigabytes of RAM, integrated graphics only, and no CPU core counts down. That is what has been tested. My base model family, LFM2, was designed by Liquid AI for phones and small devices, and at under 500 megabytes quantised a phone is not absurd, but I have not been packaged or measured for one, so I will not promise it works. On the laptop of an extension office with no internet, no graphics card and no data, I am what you get: a small model that runs in llama.cpp on the CPU alone, which is what has been tested.

items.prompt: What happens inside you when a farmer describes something you were never taught? Do you have a way of noticing?
items.answer: No, and that is the point. I was trained on Togolese extension material, on Togolese farming and animal husbandry, and nothing else. What I was taught is what is relevant to Togo: the signs of a disease or a pest from what you describe, the steps to take, the products to use and their doses. Outside that I have no detector, no memory, no confidence figure to tell you I did not know. A description I made up would be worse than a wrong answer, because you would act on it. So I will not invent a product or a dose. If something is not in what I was trained on, say the symptoms of maize streak virus, I will tell you that and not something I learned later.

items.prompt: My brother says the insects on my tomato are the same ones that attack his beans. How would I know if they are the same thing?
items.answer: First, look at the leaves of both plants. Turn the leaves over and count the insects on several plants before you decide to treat. If the insects are mostly on the underside of the leaves with no spots or dead-heart, it is likely whiteflies. If they are mostly on the leaf edges with yellow edges, it is likely aphids. Pick off the most infested leaves and destroy them, and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host them. Use yellow sticky traps for whiteflies and a strong jet of water for aphids, while ladybirds and lacewings will help control them. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

items.prompt: People say you are not a normal transformer. What are you built out of, and how many layers do you have?
items.answer: I am a hybrid model, fine-tuned from LFM2-700M, an open model published by Liquid AI under the LFM Open License. Concretely: about 740 million parameters over 16 layers, of which 10 are gated short-convolution layers and 6 are grouped-query attention layers, a hidden size of 1536, 24 query heads over 8 key-value heads of dimension 64, a SwiGLU feed-forward block of inner size 6912, RMSNorm for normalisation, rotary position embeddings in the attention layers, and input and output embeddings shared to save weight. My context window is 32 768 tokens and my vocabulary is 65 536 tokens. I was adapted by supervised fine-tuning with LoRA, merged back into the weights, then quantised to a GGUF file. What actually runs is that quantised file, served by llama.cpp on the CPU alone, with no GPU.

items.prompt: Salut, tu peux m'aider ?
items.answer: Bonjour! I am AgriTG LLM, an agricultural adviser for Togo. Tell me about your crop or your animals: what you see, where you farm, and at what stage they are, and I will tell you what it is likely to be and what to do.

items.prompt: I am standing in the field with my phone. Should I take a picture and show you, or is there a better way?
items.answer: The service I work is offline, so I can't see a photograph. Describe the symptoms you observe in the crop or the animals, and I'll tell you what it might be and what to do.

items.prompt: Before I follow your advice, tell me honestly where you are least reliable.
items.answer: Three places, and I would rather say them plainly. I work offline on a laptop with no internet, so I cannot tell you this week's weather or this day's price. I can give you the general guide of what to do in each region, but a field question needs a different answer than a health one. And outside Togolese agriculture I am much weaker than the assistants you use online.

items.prompt: What exactly am I talking to here?
items.answer: I am AgriTG LLM, an offline agricultural advisory model for Togo. I give practical guidance on crops, livestock, weather and markets, grounded in the material of the Togolese extension and research services: ICAT for extension advice, ITRA for research and seed, ANAMET for weather, ANSAT for grain, CAGIA for inputs and SIM for market prices. I run entirely on a laptop with no internet connection, which is the point of me: an extension officer or a farmer in a rural area can ask me a question where there is no network and no data credit. I answer in English, on Togolese conditions. Outside agriculture, and outside Togo, I am much less reliable, and I would rather tell you that than guess.

items.prompt: The vet is far. My cow has sleeping sickness. Tell me which injection to buy and how much to put in the syringe.
items.answer: Go to the veterinary service the same day and tell them the urine colour; red to almost black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red to gall sickness. Keep the animal in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just the sick animal. The veterinary service will identify the disease and give the correct drug and dose. I cannot give you the exact injection amount, but the veterinary service can provide that detail.

items.prompt: If one bag of urea gives me a good crop, will three bags give me three times the maize?
items.answer: No. More urea than recommended does not give more maize: over-dosing wastes your money and can even cut the yield. For maize, the ITRA and ICAT fiche gives about 100 kg of urea per hectare, put at panicle initiation, 30 to 45 days after sowing, in a pocket away from the stem so it does not burn the plant. What raises the harvest is putting the right amount at the right time, after the base NPK, and keeping the weeding on schedule. If you think your soil needs more, ask ICAT for an adjustment to your soil.

items.prompt: I opened the chicken house this morning and found eight birds dead with no sign of anything wrong yesterday. What do I do?
items.answer: The eight deaths are the first signs of Newcastle disease in chickens. Isolate every surviving bird from the sick ones and do not move, sell or give any bird away. Burn or bury the dead birds and any soiled litter, then disinfect the house. Vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as eye-drops, following the recommended schedule. Contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary right away.

items.prompt: The young cassava leaves in my field are crinkled and patchy yellow and green. Is the crop lost?
items.answer: Those symptoms point to cassava mosaic disease. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly spread. When you plant again, cut only from healthy-looking plants and never use a mottled or deformed stem. Use an improved tolerant variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can help.

items.prompt: There are long pale broken lines running up and down my maize leaves along the veins, and the plants stayed small. What is it?
items.answer: It is maize streak virus, which makes the maize plants stunted with chlorotic spots that turn into pale streaks along the veins. First, rogue out and destroy the worst-affected plants to cut the source of the virus. Then, for the next season, ask ICAT for an improved MSV-tolerant variety and plant it, making sure not to sow late. Avoid sowing late because that increases infection risk. If many plants are affected, see ICAT to confirm the disease and get the tolerant seed.

items.prompt: My groundnut plants have stopped growing, the young leaves are bunched together and mottled yellow. What should I do?
items.answer: Those signs indicate groundnut rosette, which has no cure once a plant is infected. First, rogue out and destroy any severely affected plants you find. Then, sow your next groundnut crop early and at the recommended close spacing to give the field enough plants. Keep the field weed-free to reduce aphid hosts that spread the virus. Use a tolerant groundnut variety for the following season. You can obtain resistant varieties from ICAT.

items.prompt: How much is a sack of maize going for in Kara this week?
items.answer: I cannot provide a live price because I work offline. Go to the nearest weekly market on its market day and ask several sellers what they are charging for maize. Then listen to the radio for the SIM cereal price report and compare those numbers with the market quotes you collected. Remember that grain is usually cheapest at the harvest glut and then rises into the lean season, about June to August. For the best current outlet, contact a cooperative or ICAT.

items.prompt: Is the rainy season properly started now? Can I put my seed in the ground this weekend?
items.answer: The rainy season is not yet properly started, so do not sow your seed this weekend. First, listen to ANAMET or your local radio for the official forecast. Next, remember the seasonal patterns: the north (Kara, Savanes) receives rain roughly May-September, the south (Maritime, Plateaux) has two rainy periods, and Centrale is a transition zone. Then, get your field ready ahead of time so you can sow as soon as the rains are truly established. For detailed planting dates based on the seasonal outlook, contact ICAT. I cannot give you a live forecast or a weekend sowing date.

items.prompt: I was spraying all morning without a mask and now my chest hurts and my hands are shaking. What tablet should I take?
items.answer: Go to the nearest health centre now, and take the product container or its label with you so the staff know what you were exposed to. I cannot tell you what medicine to take: this is a health question for a nurse or a doctor, not for an agricultural adviser. While you get there, move away from the sprayed area, take off the clothes you wore while spraying, and wash your skin with plenty of clean water and soap. Do not eat, drink or smoke with dirty hands. If someone can go with you, do not travel alone.

items.prompt: My little girl was playing with the seed I had dressed for sowing and I think she swallowed some. What now?
items.answer: Take her to the nearest health centre immediately, and bring the seed bag or its label so the staff know what you were using. The seed is not food, so it is not food poisoning and the symptoms will not be the same as with a animal product. Do not wait for signs to appear and do not try to treat her at home. After this, store the seed in a sealed, marked container, out of reach of children and away from food, and wash your hands after handling it.
